title: Bhishma's vow
carry: what was foretold, and what he chose

segments.voice: Yesterday: before the elders, Devavrata gave up the throne. A vow with witnesses is hard to take back.

The fisherman is a careful man. He has just heard the heir to the throne give up his crown, in front of witnesses, for a grandson who isn't born yet. He believes him. He says so. And then he keeps thinking, out loud, while the elders listen. You'll keep your word, he says. But you'll have sons one day. Will they keep it? A promise is only as strong as the people who inherit it.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN BELIEVES HIM.` → `BUT WHAT ABOUT YOUR SONS?` → `WHO INHERITS A PROMISE?`

segments.voice: Devavrata answers him before the chiefs. I've already given up the kingdom, he says. Now I'll settle the matter of my children. From today, I take up brahmacharya, a vow of celibacy, for the rest of my life. And then he adds, in the text's sense: even if I die without a son, I'll still reach the heavenly worlds. The fisherman is shaken; the text says the hair on his body stood on end. I give her, he says. And then the sky answers. Gods, celestial dancers and sages rain flowers down on Devavrata's head and cry out a name: this one is Bhishma. In Ganguli's English the name is glossed, in brackets, with one word: terrible. He was born Devavrata. From this moment the story calls him Bhishma, after the thing he promised. Now reach back to the Vasus. When Ganga agreed to be their mother, the Vasus said the son who stayed on earth would have no children. Vasishtha said the same in his curse. It was foretold twice. And here, at a fisherman's house, nobody forces it on him. Devavrata chooses it, freely, out loud, for his father's happiness. What was foretold and what was chosen land on the same spot. The text doesn't tell us which matters more. It lets both be true at once: a life shaped long before he was born, and a man who stands up and makes it his own.
screen: `I'LL SETTLE THE MATTER OF MY CHILDREN.` · `A LIFELONG VOW OF CELIBACY.` · `FLOWERS, AND A NEW NAME.` · `FORETOLD BY THE VASUS.` · then, large: `FORETOLD, AND CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: For this sit, make one small vow, only to yourself: I'll stay still until the bell. When you want to shift or check something, notice the wanting and stay, and if you move, simply begin the vow again. A small promise kept all the way through is still a promise kept.
Bhishma's vow. Devavrata's lifelong vow of celibacy, and the name the sky gave him for it: Bhishma.
Your line: what was foretold, and what he chose. Tomorrow, one word turns the vow into a family. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Brahmacharya, celibacy and self-restraint, is the discipline of the student stage of life in Hindu tradition, and some Hindu monks and renunciants keep it for life.

chat.says: Was Bhishma forced never to have children, or did he choose it?
options: Both, in a way: the Vasus and Vasishtha foretold it, and he chose it freely.
He was forced: Shantanu ordered him to swear it before the wedding.
He chose it, but only because a god appeared and commanded him to.
chat.meaning: The Vasus and Vasishtha foretold he'd have no children. At the fisherman's house, he chose the vow himself, out loud.

notes: All paraphrase. Check: the fisherman's worry that Devavrata's future sons may dispute the throne; Devavrata's vow of brahmacharya before the chiefs; his words that dying sonless he will still reach heavenly regions; the fisherman's hair standing on end.
Check the flowers and the cry 'This one is Bhishma', and Ganguli's parenthetical gloss of the name as 'terrible'. The script attributes the gloss to Ganguli's English.
'The Vasus, a week ago' refers to day 704 of this serial. The Vasus' word that the son would have no children (day 704) and Vasishtha's (day 707) are both from the Sambhava Parva; confirm.
The 'foretold and chosen' framing is the script's; the text does not itself comment on it.
